extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of natural philosophy, geology, and biology (19th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century natural-philosophy chapter arguing that single causes generate many secondary and tertiary effects, producing increasing heterogeneity across physical, geological, organic, and mental domains. The text illustrates the principle with astronomical, geological, biological, and psychological examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of effects (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplication of effects must proceed in geometrical progression. Each stage of evolution must initiate a higher stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One uniform incident force, acting on a body that becomes multiform, will itself be divided into differently modified parts; each differentiated division of the aggregate becomes a centre from which a differentiated division of the original force is again diffused, producing successive series of further differentiations and an ever-increasing heterogeneity. The author states this as a universal principle illustrated throughout astronomy, geology, biology, and psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity increases potency of secondary causes
rubrics_metrics.description: This secondary cause of the change from homogeneity to heterogeneity obviously becomes more potent in proportion as the heterogeneity increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parts of an evolving whole have diverged widely in nature they will react very diversely on an incident force, dividing that force into many strongly contrasted groups; each becomes a centre of distinct influences, multiplying secondary changes. The text emphasizes that unlike forces produce unlike results, so increased internal diversity amplifies subsequent differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and degree of unlike parts as a determinant of complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of unlike parts of which an aggregate consists, as well as the degree of their unlikeness, is an important factor in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every additional specialized division is an additional centre of specialized forces: a uniform whole made multiform makes the incident force multiform; each new unlike section is a further source of complication among the forces at work. This is presented as a quantitative and qualitative rule: both more parts and greater dissimilarity increase the multiplicative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation of diffused matter yields multiple chained effects (astronomical example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When force of aggregation acts on irregular masses of rare matter diffused through a resisting medium, masses take curvilinear paths producing rotation and oblateness, while differing condensation produces heat and sets up circulating currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent curvilinear motions of particles lead to a mass rotating about its axis (condensation and rotation). As bulk diminishes and rotation accelerates, oblateness increases; differential condensation produces variable heating; these temperature differences set up general and local circulating currents, and later light as well as heat may be generated. The chain of astronomical consequences is used to illustrate how a single aggregative force produces many distinct physical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling and contraction of planetary crust produces topographic heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: As the Earth cooled and contracted, the solid crust became too large for the shrinking nucleus, causing wrinkles that grew into hills and mountains and increased the extent and elevation of lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses the orange/tissue-paper analogy: a thin envelope wrinkles finely and evenly; a thicker envelope produces higher ridges and larger intervening spaces. As the crust thickened, lines of fracture occurred farther apart, intermediate surfaces followed the contracting nucleus less uniformly, producing larger land and water areas, more irregular coast-lines, and thus vast geological heterogeneity arising from the single cause of loss of heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solar heat transforms into diverse denuding agents depending on surface heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The sun's rays, striking a sphere with atmosphere and varied surface conditions, initiate countless different motions—air and marine currents, precipitation forms, freezing and thawing—leading to a wide variety of denuding results determined by local circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transformation of solar heat into different modes of force varies according to the nature and condition of the matter acted upon; oxidation, drought, wind, frost, rain, glaciers, rivers, and waves produce disintegrations whose amounts and qualities are locally determined. Examples: the same denuding agents produce little effect on granite in one place, exfoliation and boulder heaps in another, and decomposition to clay in a third. The principle: the more heterogeneous the object acted on, the more heterogeneous the results (geometric progression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex pre-existing structure multiplies the effects of later disturbances
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complicated area is acted upon by a force (e.g., a planet or geological revolution), the direct perturbations lead to secondary and tertiary perturbations among interacting parts, producing ever-multiplying waves of smaller but numerous consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by planetary perturbations: planet A perturbs B; B's altered position changes perturbations it exerts on others, producing secondary and tertiary series of effects. Similarly, a major geologic event such as the subsidence of Central America would cause immediate complex effects (dislocations, ejections, waves) and long-term permanent alterations (ocean currents, heat distribution, tides, winds, rainfall) over vast regions. The rule: complexity of initial conditions greatly magnifies the downstream multiplicity of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of effects in organismal (embryonic) development—epigenesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In embryonic development, successive transformations occur because agencies act on the partial organization present at each stage, producing further complications; no germ contains explicit rudiments of the future form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given that a fertilized germ begins as repeated spontaneous fissions yielding undifferentiated cells, the partial organization at any moment is transformed by external and internal agencies into the next phase. Each newly formed organ influences nutrition, blood composition, nervous connections, and waste products, which in turn initiate further developments. The author invokes epigenesis to argue that multiplication of effects (one change generating many others) is intrinsic to organic evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single stimuli produce numerous physiological and pathological effects
rubrics_metrics.description: An alarming sound or sight, or a minute quantity of a virus, produces multiple bodily responses across systems—sensory impressions, muscular reactions, cardiac changes, secretions, fevers, and possibly long illnesses—each with further subsidiary complexities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples used: startling stimuli can cause a start, scream, facial distortion, trembling, perspiration, cardiac acceleration, cerebral blood rush, syncope, and longer illness. Small-pox virus causes multi-stage symptom sets; medicines or improved air likewise produce many changes. The point: macro-multiplication of effects is visible even in single-organism responses, and similar multiplicative cascades occur in embryos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence and speciation via successive environmental and habit changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated geological revolutions and resulting environmental diversifications cause an original species to give rise to several divergent varieties or species; dispersion and distinct local conditions increase chances of survival for some derivatives and occasionally yield higher (more heterogeneous) forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by raising an archipelago into a continent: first upheaval slightly modifies conditions producing local modifications of flora and fauna; subsequent upheavals add further changes; migration into differing zones (shores versus mountains) causes distinct adaptive modifications. The author emphasizes that instead of one-to-one substitution, the thousand original species may give rise to several thousand varieties/species, some of which occasionally become more heterogeneous (higher). The passage notes that natural selection (Darwin) would later be used to explain facilitation of such differentiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and historical causes multiply biological and cultural variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Single social causes (famine, population pressure, war) periodically lead to dispersions of people and dependent organisms, each dispersion initiating new modifications and varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author applies the principle to human races and domestic animals: dispersal into different climates and treatments produces local differences and new breeds (e.g., sheep, cattle). Human migrations and cultural separations produce linguistic and racial divergences. The guidance is to see sociocultural forces as agents whose single occurrences generate manifold biological and cultural consequences over generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher intelligence multiplies mental associations from a sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: A sensation does not arouse a single state of consciousness; the state prompted comprises various represented sensations connected by coexistence or sequence, and in proportion to the grade of intelligence the number of ideas suggested is great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author claims that mental multiplication mirrors physical and biological multiplication of effects: as intelligence increases, a presented sensation suggests many ideas (associations), producing complex cognitive states. This is offered as an extension of the general causal-multiplication principle into psychology and consciousness studies.
